strengths: The paper formalizes a novel and practically important 'meta-AFA' problem, generalizing single-task active feature acquisition to a setting where a policy is learned across a distribution of tasks with retrospective, task-varying missingness, and provides a clean causal-identifiability argument (Theorem 3.4) specifying the MAR/exclusion-restriction/positivity conditions under which the CMI objective is estimable from observed data alone.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves (Proposition A.2 and its meta extension Theorem 4.2) that minimizing the proposed one-step surrogate sequence-modeling loss recovers both a Bayes-optimal predictor and a CMI-optimal greedy acquisition policy, connecting the practical training objective to the stated CMI goal rather than leaving this as a heuristic.

The architecture thoughtfully adapts a transformer for AFA: removing positional encodings, introducing context/target/query token types, and designing a custom attention mask to satisfy the context-invariance and target-equivariance properties needed for valid in-context Bayesian-style inference, plus a Gumbel-softmax relaxation enabling fully differentiable end-to-end policy training.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning fully synthetic GP regression, semi-synthetic classification built on real feature distributions (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and a real-image task (MNIST), with multiple relevant task-specific baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN) and useful ablations on context length, missingness rate, and the value of instance-wise adaptivity.

The reproducibility appendix is detailed (architecture hyperparameters, training algorithms, preprocessing, baseline configurations, compute/runtime information), and limitations (reliance on MAR/positivity, reliance on synthetic/semi-synthetic task priors, restriction to time-invariant settings) are honestly and specifically discussed.
weaknesses: The core methodological ingredients (transformer/PFN-style in-context Bayesian sequence modeling for uncertainty quantification, and greedy CMI-based one-step surrogate acquisition from Covert et al. 2023) are both adapted from existing work; the main novelty is their combination for the meta-AFA setting rather than a fundamentally new estimation or decision-making principle, which somewhat limits originality.

Empirical gains are inconsistent: the paper itself reports that 'adaptive strategies offer only marginal gains over random acquisition on some real datasets' and that real-task uncertainty-quantification improvements are 'mixed' (Figure 8), which weakens the significance claims relative to the strength of the theoretical framing.

The 'meta' tasks used for pretraining on real datasets are semi-synthetic, generated via BNN-prior label functions over real feature distributions rather than genuinely heterogeneous real-world tasks/labels; this raises concern about how well results generalize to true cross-task diversity as claimed by the meta-AFA framing (MIMIC with real labels is the only case with authentic task heterogeneity, and even there gains are modest for some outcomes such as Readmission).

All baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN, MLP) are strictly single-task models trained from scratch; there is no comparison to any other transfer-learning or pretrained baseline that shares information across tasks, making it hard to disentangle how much of L2M's advantage stems from meta-learning/in-context transfer per se versus simply using a larger, better-regularized transformer architecture.

Experiments are limited to relatively low feature dimensionality (d=10–20) and moderate sequence/context lengths; scalability of the in-context transformer approach (compute/memory, and acquisition quality) to higher-dimensional feature spaces or larger acquisition budgets typical of many real AFA applications is not empirically investigated.

The identifiability assumptions (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity) underlying the theoretical guarantees are strong and untestable in real retrospective clinical data; while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper does not empirically probe sensitivity to violations of these assumptions, leaving the practical robustness of the identification result unclear.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and theoretical apparatus in the main text, and the connection between the elaborate theory and the practical experimental takeaways could be made more explicit and accessible.

strengths: The meta-AFA formulation is a reasonable and underexplored framing of active feature acquisition that could enable amortized, cross-task deployment instead of per-task retraining.

The paper provides a careful causal-identifiability treatment of CMI estimation under retrospective missingness (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity), giving the method a principled theoretical grounding rather than relying purely on heuristic imputation.

Theorem 4.2 extends the one-step surrogate optimality result of Covert et al. (2023) to the sequence-modeling/in-context setting with a full proof, connecting the policy optimization objective to CMI-maximizing greedy acquisition.

Experiments span a reasonably wide set of settings (synthetic GP regression with RBF/Matern kernels, MNIST, and several real tabular/clinical datasets including MIMIC-IV with real labels), with ablations on context length, missingness rate, and the value of instance-level adaptivity.
Reasonably detailed appendix with architecture, training algorithms, and hyperparameters supporting partial reproducibility, along with a stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: The empirical benefits are inconsistent and often marginal on real datasets; the authors themselves note 'adaptive strategies offer only marginal gains over random acquisition on some real datasets,' which undercuts the paper's central significance claim that L2M 'matches or surpasses' task-specific baselines broadly.

The method's advantage is explicitly contingent on how well the hand-designed pretraining task prior (BNN logits, GP kernels) aligns with the downstream task distribution; this shifts the burden from per-task retraining to prior/task-distribution design, which is not automated, justified, or evaluated for robustness/misspecification, weakening the 'foundation-model paradigm' framing.

Most 'real-world' evaluations (Metabric, MiniBooNE) actually use semi-synthetic labels generated from a BNN prior rather than true task labels, and feature/task dimensionality tested is small (d ≤ 20), making claims of scalability and real-world applicability only weakly supported.

Several baselines (GDFS, DIME) are deliberately trained with simplified procedures that diverge from their original papers (fixed-temperature Gumbel-softmax instead of decay schedules, random acquisition instead of epsilon-greedy for DIME's reward predictor), raising concerns about whether the baseline comparisons are tuned fairly or systematically disadvantaged relative to L2M.

No statistically grounded comparison (e.g., significance tests) is provided despite overlapping error bands in several key figures (e.g., MIMIC mortality/readmission panels in Fig. 4), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are meaningful versus noise.

Key theoretical assumptions underlying the method (missing-at-random, positivity, exclusion restriction, and conditional independence across queries in Assumption A.5) are untestable in practice and not empirically stress-tested (e.g., under MNAR or correlated query settings), despite the paper's claims of principled handling of 'arbitrary missingness.'

The identification theorem (Thm 3.4) is a relatively direct application of standard missing-data/causal-identification results (Rubin-style assumptions), and the main algorithmic novelty largely consists of combining known building blocks (sequence-model-based Bayesian inference à la TNP/PFN, Gumbel-softmax policy relaxation, and CMI-based greedy acquisition from Covert et al.), limiting the degree of methodological originality.

No comparison is made to stronger generative/latent-variable AFA baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Li & Oliva 2021, Gong et al. 2019, Peis et al. 2022), leaving open whether the reported gains hold against more competitive alternatives.

strengths: Formalizes a well-motivated and underexplored problem (meta-AFA across tasks with retrospective missingness), connecting active feature acquisition to the in-context learning / sequence-modeling literature, which is a timely and useful reframing.

Provides a rigorous causal identification argument (Theorem 3.4) for estimating CMI from retrospectively missing data under MAR, exclusion restriction, and positivity, giving the method principled theoretical grounding rather than purely heuristic imputation.

Theorem 4.2 extends prior greedy-CMI surrogate-optimality results (Covert et al., 2023) to the in-context/meta setting, showing the joint predictor-policy objective recovers per-query Bayes-optimal predictions and CMI-maximizing actions; proofs are provided in detail in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning synthetic GP regression (RBF/Matern), semi-synthetic classification derived from real tabular data (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV with three distinct clinical tasks), and MNIST, with consistent comparisons against task-specific greedy (GDFS, DIME) and RL (DQN) baselines.

Useful ablations isolating the effect of context length, missingness rate, and the value of instance-level adaptivity versus static/random acquisition, which help clarify when and why the method helps.

Reasonable effort toward reproducibility: detailed architecture description (custom attention masking, context/target/query encoding), training algorithms, hyperparameters, and dataset preprocessing are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: Several real-world results show only marginal improvement over random acquisition or baselines (as the authors themselves note for some datasets), raising questions about the practical significance of the approach outside of the synthetic/semi-synthetic BNN-prior setting that closely matches the pretraining distribution.

The pretraining task prior (BNN-generated labels over real feature distributions) is itself synthetic, so evaluation on 'real-world' datasets still partly tests the model's ability to generalize from one synthetic generative family to another rather than genuine cross-task transfer in the wild; the paper acknowledges this as future work but it limits current significance claims.

No comparison to generative/latent-variable AFA baselines (e.g., EDDI, ACFlow, Li & Oliva's generative surrogate models) that are discussed at length in related work, despite these being the main alternative class of methods for handling missingness in AFA.

The theoretical optimality result (Theorem 4.2) is a population-level statement about joint minimizers; there is no finite-sample or approximation-error analysis characterizing behavior when the transformer does not reach the global optimum, which is the realistic regime in all experiments.

Scalability is not empirically demonstrated: all experiments use small feature sets (d=10–20); it is unclear how inference cost (a forward pass over the full context for every query at every acquisition step) and model quality scale to higher-dimensional, larger real datasets typical of healthcare applications motivating the paper.

Reporting of variance (e.g., 'standard error across 200 sampled evaluation tasks') does not clarify whether this reflects multiple independently trained models or a single trained model evaluated on many tasks, leaving training-stochasticity-driven variance unaddressed.

The MAR/positivity assumptions underlying the core identification result are strong and explicitly untestable; while honestly flagged as a limitation, no sensitivity analysis or diagnostic is provided to gauge robustness to violations, despite real clinical missingness often being MNAR.

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.4 establishes identifiability of the CMI acquisition objective under retrospective missingness (MAR, no direct effect, positivity), connecting AFA to the causal missing-data/off-policy evaluation literature in a way prior AFA work largely ignores.

Theorem 4.2 rigorously shows that the proposed sequence-modeling surrogate loss, when minimized, recovers both a Bayes-optimal predictor and a CMI-optimal (blocked) acquisition policy, giving the empirical method a clear theoretical justification rather than being purely heuristic.

The core idea of casting AFA as an in-context/meta-learning problem via an exchangeable-sequence transformer is a novel and well-motivated combination of existing threads (PFN-style Bayesian ICL and CMI-based greedy AFA), addressing a real practical gap (single-task retraining, task-specific generative models).

Extensive experimental suite spanning synthetic GP/BNN tasks, real tabular datasets (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and MNIST, with multiple complementary uncertainty metrics (coverage, NLL, Brier, KL, AUROC) and sensible baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN).

Thorough appendix ablations: robustness to context length and missingness rate, lookahead vs greedy policies, gradient-estimator quality vs REINFORCE and IPW baselines, and a CNP-style meta-learning ablation, which substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond the main text.
Honest and specific limitations section (untestable MAR/positivity, no cost-sensitive MDP, time-invariance restriction, scale) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: The central MAR / no-direct-effect / positivity assumptions are strong and, as acknowledged, untestable; many realistic clinical missingness mechanisms (e.g., ordering a test because a clinician suspects an abnormal but unobserved value) plausibly violate MAR, which undercuts the generality of the identifiability guarantee that underpins the whole framework.

Real-world empirical results are mixed: Figure 8 explicitly shows uncertainty-quantification gains over the MLP baseline are inconsistent on real, unseen labels, and the fully-synthetic pretrained variant (L2M-Syn) needs task-specific fine-tuning to be competitive (Fig. 14), which partially undermines the paper's central claim of eliminating per-task retraining.

Baseline implementations are modified from their original papers in ways that could disadvantage them (e.g., DIME trained with random rather than epsilon-greedy acquisition, GDFS with fixed rather than annealed temperature), raising concerns about the fairness of the head-to-head comparisons.

Precision/recall analysis (Appendix Figs. 12–13) shows the task-specific baseline is more precise at identifying truly informative features than L2M, suggesting the meta-learned policy sometimes hedges rather than sharply ranking features—an important caveat to the headline claim of superior acquisition quality that is somewhat downplayed in the main text.

Experiments are limited to small-to-medium scale tabular settings (10–20 candidate features, datasets of a few thousand samples); scalability to larger feature spaces/datasets or to a true foundation-model backbone (e.g., TabPFN) is left entirely to future work, so the foundation-model framing in the introduction is aspirational rather than demonstrated.

The task prior (BNN/GP-based data generating processes) must be hand-specified, and performance depends heavily on how well this prior matches the deployment task; the paper does not provide much guidance on how to choose/validate priors for new domains, which limits practical reproducibility outside the tested benchmarks.

The dense theoretical exposition (proofs, multiple assumptions, blocked policies, Gumbel-softmax relaxations) is not always clearly connected back to intuitive takeaways in the main text, making the paper harder to parse for readers focused on practical AFA deployment.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: active feature acquisition under retrospective (historical) missingness, combined with a meta-learning/in-context formulation that could in principle avoid costly per-task retraining.

The theoretical treatment is reasonably careful: Theorem 3.4 gives a clean potential-outcomes-based identification result for CMI under MAR/no-direct-effect/positivity assumptions, and Theorem 4.2 (with detailed appendix proofs) shows that the proposed sequence-loss minimizer recovers both a Bayes-optimal predictor and the CMI-maximizing acquisition policy, tying the practical algorithm to the stated theoretical objective.

The empirical evaluation is extensive in breadth: synthetic GP/BNN tasks, a lookahead variant for non-submodular settings, several real tabular datasets (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV) and MNIST, plus a large number of appendix ablations (calibration curves, context-length/missingness sensitivity, gradient-estimator quality vs. REINFORCE/IPW, meta-learning ablations against CNP-style approaches).

The limitations section is candid about the reliance on MAR/positivity, the use of synthetic pretraining priors, and the restriction to time-invariant, medium-scale tabular settings, which is good practice.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim—handling retrospective missingness—is never actually tested in the main results. All 'real-world' experiments inject a synthetic missingness mechanism on top of real covariates/labels; the only evaluation under genuine real-world missingness (MIMIC-IV, Appendix Fig. 16) is explicitly flagged by the authors as a 'stress test, not a definitive measure of deployment performance' due to confounded context–query distribution shift. This leaves the paper's core problem statement empirically unvalidated.

The headline contribution of 'eliminating per-task retraining' is undercut by the authors' own appendix results: the fully-synthetic pretrained variant (L2M-Syn) degrades substantially on real tasks and only becomes competitive after task-specific gradient fine-tuning (Fig. 14), which is precisely the per-task retraining the method claims to avoid. This tension is not reconciled in the main text.

Baseline implementations deviate from the original papers in ways that could weaken them (e.g., GDFS trained with fixed Gumbel-softmax temperature instead of the published annealing schedule; DIME trained with random rather than epsilon-greedy acquisitions), raising concerns about whether the reported margins over GDFS/DIME/DQN reflect genuine methodological advantages or weakened baselines.

The meta-learning advantage is partly confounded with unequal training budgets/data exposure: L2M is pretrained on large volumes of diverse synthetic tasks (up to 100k steps across many tasks) while task-specific baselines are trained with comparatively modest budgets per single task (300/50 epochs); the paper does not isolate how much of the improvement is attributable to architecture/objective versus sheer extra compute and task diversity seen at train time.

Performance gains are explicitly acknowledged to depend on how well the hand-crafted synthetic task prior (BNN/GP) matches the downstream task, and the real evaluations are capped at modest dimensionality (≤20 features); scaling to larger, more realistic tabular settings is left entirely to speculative future work (e.g., citing TabPFN as a 'plausible' direction without any experiments).

Precision/recall diagnostics (Fig. 12–13) show that the task-specific baseline is sometimes more precise at identifying truly informative features even when L2M's log-loss/AUROC is better, suggesting the gains may partly reflect better-calibrated averaging rather than uniformly superior feature-targeting, a nuance underexplored in the main text.

The paper is dense and proof-heavy relative to the depth of empirical validation of its most novel practical claims (in-context, no-retraining AFA under real missingness), making the presentation feel oriented toward justifying a method whose central use case is not convincingly demonstrated.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: the paper provides a causal identification result for conditional mutual information under retrospective missingness (Theorem 3.4, with explicit MAR, no-direct-effect, and positivity assumptions and a full proof), and a second theorem (4.2, with detailed proof in the appendix) showing that minimizing the proposed sequence-modeling surrogate loss recovers both the Bayes-optimal predictor and the CMI-optimal greedy/lookahead acquisition policy. This grounds the empirical method in principled statistical/causal reasoning rather than purely heuristic design.

Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: most AFA work assumes complete training data or uses naive imputation; this paper explicitly models retrospective missingness and formalizes when AFA policies are identifiable from observational data, which is practically important for healthcare-style deployment.

The meta-learning/in-context formulation is a meaningful departure from the task-specific paradigm dominant in prior AFA literature (GDFS, DIME, EDDI, RL-based methods), enabling a single pretrained model to generalize across tasks without retraining, aligned with the foundation-model direction.

Extensive and varied empirical evaluation: synthetic GP regression and BNN classification (including a deliberately non-submodular BNN-Plan setting to test lookahead benefits), semi-synthetic tasks on Metabric/MiniBooNE/MIMIC-IV, and MNIST block-acquisition, compared against multiple credible baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN).

Thorough ablations in the appendix: calibration/coverage analysis, sensitivity to context length and missingness rate, pathwise vs. REINFORCE vs. IPW gradient-estimator quality/bias/variance comparisons, meta-learning architecture ablations (CNP-style pooling), zero-shot generalization from fully synthetic pretraining to real data, and qualitative policy visualizations — this depth strengthens confidence in the claims.

The differentiable Gumbel-softmax relaxation for end-to-end joint training of predictor and policy is a reasonable and clearly described engineering contribution that avoids expensive REINFORCE-style estimation, with empirical evidence (Fig. 17, Table 5) that it is substantially more sample-efficient than REINFORCE or IPW alternatives.
Honest and specific limitations/impact discussion (untestable MAR assumption, short-horizon planning, time-invariant restriction, scale) rather than a generic boilerplate statement.
weaknesses: The benefit of meta-learning on genuinely unseen real-world tasks is mixed rather than uniformly positive (Figure 8, Appendix A.8.1), and the fully-synthetic pretrained variant (L2M-Syn) degrades substantially when applied zero-shot to real data, requiring task-specific fine-tuning to recover competitive performance (Figure 14) — this partially undercuts the central claim that L2M eliminates per-task retraining in practice.

Real-world evaluation scale is modest: MIMIC-IV experiments use only ~5,000 training rows, 3 tasks, and at most ~15-20 acquirable features; it remains unclear how the approach scales to larger, higher-dimensional, more heterogeneous tabular settings typical of real deployment (acknowledged as future work using e.g. TabPFN-scale architectures, but not tested).

Pretraining task priors (BNN, GP) are comparatively simple hand-designed generative mechanisms; the model is effectively retrained per dataset family rather than using one truly universal pretrained backbone, so the 'foundation model' framing is somewhat aspirational relative to what is demonstrated.

Baselines are all MLP/single-model task-specific methods; no comparison is made against other in-context/meta-learning uncertainty approaches (e.g., TabPFN-based predictors as oracles) that might also provide strong calibrated uncertainty without the full L2M pipeline, making it harder to isolate which component (sequence-model UQ vs. the policy-learning mechanism) drives the gains.

The MAR/no-direct-effect/positivity assumptions underlying the core identification theorem are acknowledged as untestable and are not empirically stress-tested except for a single informal 'stress test' on real MIMIC-IV missingness patterns (Appendix A.8.2), which the authors themselves caution should be interpreted carefully due to confounded distribution shift.

Precision/recall analyses on synthetic tasks with known ground-truth informative features (Figures 12-13) show the task-specific baseline is sometimes more precise at identifying truly informative features, suggesting the meta-learned policy may sacrifice some sharpness for better calibrated uncertainty, a trade-off that is not fully explored or discussed.
